                                   1

                                   2

                                   3                                  UNITED STATES DISTRICT COURT

                                   4                              NORTHERN DISTRICT OF CALIFORNIA

                                   5                                         SAN JOSE DIVISION

                                   6

                                   7        ERICA L ZAPIEN,                                 Case No. 25-cv-00387-BLF
                                   8                     Plaintiff,
                                                  v.                                        ORDER RE MOTIONS IN LIMINE
                                   9
                                            FCA US, LLC,                                    [Re: ECF Nos. 30, 31, 32, 33]
                                  10
                                                         Defendant.
                                  11

                                  12
Northern District of California
 United States District Court




                                  13

                                  14            Before the Court are Defendant FCA US, LLC’s (“FCA”) four motions in limine

                                  15   (“MILs”). See ECF Nos. 30, 31, 32, 33. The Court held the Final Pretrial Conference on August

                                  16   20, 2026, and issued oral rulings on FCA’s MILs. See ECF No. 56. The Court subsequently
                                  17
                                       issued an order setting trial schedule and procedures. See ECF No. 57. For the reasons stated by
                                  18
                                       the Court on the record at the hearing and set forth below, the Court rules on FCA’s MILs as
                                  19
                                       follows.
                                  20
                                       I.       BACKGROUND
                                  21

                                  22            On or about September 20, 2021, Plaintiff Erica Zapien entered into a warranty contract

                                  23   with FCA regarding a new 2021 RAM 2500 (the “Subject Vehicle”). ECF No. 1-1 at ¶ 7. The
                                  24   warranty contract contained several express warranties covering various aspects of the Subject
                                  25
                                       Vehicle. Id. at ¶ 8, Ex. A at 7–11.
                                  26
                                                Ms. Zapien alleges that during the warranty period, the Subject Vehicle began to manifest
                                  27
                                       signs of potential defects and nonconformities to the warranty. Id. at ¶ 12. Ms. Zapien asserts that
                                  28
                                            Case 5:25-cv-00387-BLF         Document 58        Filed 08/26/26     Page 2 of 9




                                       she presented the Subject Vehicle to FCA’s authorized service representatives, but after a number
                                   1

                                   2   of attempts, they were unable to repair the nonconformities. ECF No. 21 at 3. On August 30,

                                   3   2024, Ms. Zapien initiated this action in state court, alleging that FCA violated its express and

                                   4   implied warranty obligations. See ECF No. 1-1. Ms. Zapien’s complaint alleges multiple
                                   5
                                       violations of the Song-Beverly Consumer Warranty Act (“Song-Beverly Act”), California Civil
                                   6
                                       Code §§ 1791.1, 1793.2(b), 1793.2(d).1 Id. at ¶¶ 20–53. This action was removed to federal court
                                   7
                                       on January 10, 2025. See ECF No. 1.
                                   8
                                       II.      LEGAL STANDARD
                                   9

                                  10            Under Federal Rule of Evidence 401, “[e]vidence is relevant if: (a) it has any tendency to

                                  11   make a fact more or less probable than it would be without the evidence; and (b) the fact is of
                                  12   consequence in determining the action.” Fed. R. Evid. 401. “[R]elevant evidence is admissible
Northern District of California
 United States District Court




                                  13
                                       unless another rule or federal law provides otherwise,” while “irrelevant evidence is inadmissible.”
                                  14
                                       Crawford v. City of Bakersfield, 944 F.3d 1070, 1077 (9th Cir. 2019); accord Fed. R. Evid. 402
                                  15
                                       (providing that relevant evidence is admissible unless precluded by the Constitution, federal
                                  16

                                  17   statute, the federal rules of evidence, or a rule prescribed by the Supreme Court). Rule 401’s

                                  18   “basic standard of relevance . . . is a liberal one.” Crawford, 944 F.3d at 1077 (alteration in

                                  19   original) (quoting Daubert v. Merrell Dow Pharms., Inc., 509 U.S. 579, 587 (1993)). “The court
                                  20   may exclude relevant evidence if its probative value is substantially outweighed by a danger of
                                  21
                                       one or more of the following: unfair prejudice, confusing the issues, misleading the jury, undue
                                  22
                                       delay, wasting time, or needlessly presenting cumulative evidence.” Fed. R. Evid. 403; see also
                                  23
                                       United States v. LeMay, 260 F.3d 1018, 1027 (9th Cir. 2001).
                                  24

                                  25

                                  26
                                       1
                                           Ms. Zapien’s complaint also included a claim under Cal. Civ. Code § 1793.2(a)(3), but she has
                                  27
                                       since withdrawn that claim. ECF No. 36 at 3.
                                  28
                                                                                         2
                                          Case 5:25-cv-00387-BLF             Document 58         Filed 08/26/26     Page 3 of 9




                                       III.   DISCUSSION
                                   1

                                   2          A. MIL No. 1 to Exclude Reference, Evidence, Testimony, or Argument Relating to
                                                 Complaints that Were Resolved After the First Repair Attempt
                                   3
                                              In its MIL No. 1, FCA moves to exclude argument and evidence of complaints concerning
                                   4
                                       the Subject Vehicle that were resolved after the first repair attempt. ECF No. 30. FCA contends
                                   5

                                   6   that under Cal. Civ. Code § 1793.2(d)(2), Ms. Zapien must prove that FCA’s representatives failed

                                   7   to repair the Subject Vehicle “after a reasonable number of attempts.” Id. at 2. Based on this

                                   8   requirement, FCA argues that evidence of one-time complaints would confuse the issues and
                                   9   mislead the jury. Id. In particular, MIL No. 1 seeks to exclude evidence of the following
                                  10
                                       complaints: (1) the portion of Repair Order 115133 relating to the “throttle light turning on,” (2)
                                  11
                                       the portion of Repair Order 288741 pertaining to the Subject Vehicle’s “horn honking on its own,”
                                  12
Northern District of California
 United States District Court




                                       (3) the portion of Repair Order 286834 concerning “the engine making noise and losing power,”
                                  13

                                  14   and (4) the related portion of Repair Order 288741, in which FCA’s representative installed the

                                  15   part necessary to address the engine complaint. Id. at 3–4.

                                  16          In opposition, Ms. Zapien argues that “[m]odern vehicle systems are interconnected” such
                                  17
                                       that lay consumers often cannot tell whether multiple issues are caused by the same underlying
                                  18
                                       defect. ECF No. 50 at 2–3. She further asserts that one-time complaints are independently
                                  19
                                       relevant to her claims brought under Cal. Civ. Code §§ 1791.1, 1793.2(b). Id. at 3.
                                  20
                                              Under Cal. Civ. Code § 1793.2(d)(2), Ms. Zapien has the burden to prove that
                                  21

                                  22                     (1) the vehicle had a nonconformity covered by the express warranty
                                                         that substantially impaired the use, value or safety of the vehicle (the
                                  23                     nonconformity element); (2) the vehicle was presented to an
                                                         authorized representative of the manufacturer of the vehicle for repair
                                  24                     (the presentation element); and (3) the manufacturer or his
                                                         representative did not repair the nonconformity after a reasonable
                                  25                     number of repair attempts (the failure to repair element).

                                  26   Donlen v. Ford Motor Co., 217 Cal. App. 4th 138, 152 (2013), as modified on denial of reh’g

                                  27   (July 8, 2013).
                                  28
                                                                                            3
                                         Case 5:25-cv-00387-BLF           Document 58         Filed 08/26/26    Page 4 of 9




                                              FCA is correct that § 1793.2(d)(2) applies only to defects that were subject to multiple
                                   1

                                   2   repair attempts. Silvio v. Ford Motor Co., 109 Cal. App. 4th 1205, 1209 (2003), as modified (June

                                   3   19, 2003) (“[T]he statute indicates that even where the defect is life-threatening, one opportunity
                                   4   to repair is not enough.”). However, as Ms. Zapien notes, one-time complaints may be relevant
                                   5
                                       for determining whether the Subject Vehicle was repaired “after a reasonable number of attempts.”
                                   6
                                       See ECF No. 50 at 2.
                                   7

                                   8          As was discussed at the hearing, modern vehicles are interconnected. So, seemingly

                                   9   unrelated issues, such as Ms. Zapien’s horn complaints and throttle light complaints, may be

                                  10   caused by the same underlying electrical defect. Under those circumstances, evidence of
                                  11
                                       Ms. Zapien’s various complaints would be highly relevant to determining whether FCA repaired
                                  12
Northern District of California




                                       the source of the nonconformity after multiple attempts. Cf. Robertson v. Fleetwood Travel
 United States District Court




                                  13
                                       Trailers of California, Inc., 144 Cal. App. 4th 785, 801 (2006) (upholding the jury’s determination
                                  14

                                  15   that the defendant “failed to repair the nonconformity after a reasonable number of attempts”

                                  16   where the defendant cured the source of the nonconformity but did not fix “the entirety of the
                                  17
                                       problem”). If, in the alternative, the evidence presented tends to show that Ms. Zapien’s one-time
                                  18
                                       complaints were isolated incidents, unrelated to any other defect, then FCA may object to
                                  19
                                       evidence of these complaints at trial.
                                  20

                                  21          The Court also agrees with Ms. Zapien that her one-time complaints are relevant to her

                                  22   claims under Cal. Civ. Code §§ 1791.1, 1793.2(b). To succeed on a claim under § 1791.1,
                                  23
                                       otherwise known as the implied warranty of merchantability, plaintiffs must demonstrate (1) that
                                  24
                                       the purchased goods were not “fit for the ordinary purposes for which such goods are used,” (2)
                                  25
                                       causation, and (3) damages. Carver v. Volkswagen Grp. of Am., Inc., 107 Cal. App. 5th 864, 888–
                                  26
                                  27   89 (quoting Cal. Civ. Code § 1791.1(a)(2)). Unlike § 1793.2(d)(2), the implied warranty of

                                  28   merchantability does not require the claimant to provide the defendant with multiple opportunities
                                                                                         4
                                         Case 5:25-cv-00387-BLF            Document 58          Filed 08/26/26    Page 5 of 9




                                       to repair the alleged defect. See id. at 878 (clarifying that § 1791.1 does not require the plaintiff to
                                   1

                                   2   “present the defective vehicle to an authorized representative . . . for repair and give the

                                   3   manufacturer a reasonable opportunity to fix the vehicle”). Therefore, evidence of one-time
                                   4   complaints is relevant to Ms. Zapien’s § 1791.1 claim because it tends to prove whether the
                                   5
                                       Subject Vehicle was fit for its ordinary purpose.
                                   6
                                              Section § 1793.2(b) similarly lacks any requirement that the alleged nonconformities were
                                   7

                                   8   subject to multiple attempted repairs. Section § 1793.2(b) provides that where a vehicle does “not

                                   9   conform with the applicable express warranties, service and repair shall be commenced within a

                                  10   reasonable time” and the vehicle “shall be serviced or repaired so as to conform to the applicable
                                  11
                                       warranties within 30 days.” Cal. Civ. Code § 1793.2(b). Accordingly, evidence of one-time
                                  12
Northern District of California




                                       complaints may be relevant to determining whether FCA’s authorized representatives commenced
 United States District Court




                                  13
                                       and completed the repairs within the required timeframe.
                                  14

                                  15          For these reasons, FCA’s MIL No. 1 to exclude evidence of complaints that were repaired

                                  16   after one service attempt is DENIED without prejudice to reasserting the objection in response to
                                  17
                                       specific evidence presented at trial.
                                  18
                                              B. MIL No. 2 to Exclude Evidence, Testimony, or Argument Relating to Complaints
                                  19             that Plaintiff Did Not Present to FCA or FCA’s Authorized Representatives
                                  20          MIL No. 2 seeks to exclude evidence and testimony of alleged defects that Ms. Zapien
                                  21
                                       never presented to FCA or its authorized representatives. ECF No. 31. FCA asserts that under the
                                  22
                                       Song-Beverly Act, Ms. Zapien was required to present her concerns to FCA or an authorized
                                  23
                                       repair facility so that they could have a “reasonable opportunity to repair the vehicle.” Id. at 2
                                  24

                                  25   (quoting Oregel v. Am. Isuzu Motors, Inc., 90 Cal. App. 4th 1094, 1103 (2001)). FCA argues that

                                  26   allowing Ms. Zapien to admit evidence of defects that she never presented to a repair shop would
                                  27
                                       mislead the jury and cause unfair prejudice. Id.
                                  28
                                                                                           5
                                         Case 5:25-cv-00387-BLF           Document 58         Filed 08/26/26     Page 6 of 9




                                              Ms. Zapien contends that FCA’s argument fails because lay consumers are not responsible
                                   1

                                   2   for “identify[ing] the technical cause of a” defect. ECF No. 51 at 2. Her opposition posits that a

                                   3   consumer may, for example, present an “engine noise” complaint to the manufacturer but lack the
                                   4   technical awareness and terminology necessary to identify the underlying “transmission” defect.
                                   5
                                       Id. Ms. Zapien argues that consumers should not be faulted for failing to properly present such
                                   6
                                       defects because it is the manufacturer’s responsibility to identify and resolve the source of the
                                   7

                                   8   consumer’s complaint. Id. at 2–3. Accordingly, she asserts that evidence of unreported

                                   9   complaints should be admitted because it tends to prove whether she sufficiently presented the

                                  10   defects and whether the manufacturer made adequate repairs. Id. at 3. Ms. Zapien further
                                  11
                                       maintains that evidence of unreported claims should be admitted because presentation is not a
                                  12
Northern District of California




                                       required element of the implied warranty of merchantability. Id. at 3.
 United States District Court




                                  13
                                              Section 1793.2(d)(2)’s presentation element requires that the complaint “was presented to
                                  14

                                  15   an authorized representative of the manufacturer of the vehicle for repair.” Donlen, 217 Cal. App.

                                  16   4th at 152. Where a plaintiff fails to present a complaint, she effectively deprives the authorized
                                  17
                                       representative of the opportunity to make a “reasonable number of attempts” to repair the issue.
                                  18
                                       See Cal Civ. Code § 1793.2(d)(2). Therefore, admitting this evidence risks misleading the jury by
                                  19
                                       causing them to conflate defects that FCA’s representatives were obligated to repair with defects
                                  20

                                  21   that the representatives were entirely unaware of. For this reason, the Court agrees GRANTS

                                  22   FCA’s MIL No. 2 as to Ms. Zapien’s § 1793.2(d)(2) claim.
                                  23
                                              However, Ms. Zapien is correct that the implied warranty of merchantability does not
                                  24
                                       require plaintiffs to present alleged defects to the manufacturer. See § 1791.1; Carver, 107 Cal.
                                  25
                                       App. 5th at 878 (noting that while express warranty claims require the plaintiff to “present the
                                  26
                                  27   defective vehicle to an authorized representative,” implied warranty claims have no such

                                  28   requirement). Provided that the defects satisfy § 1791.1(c)’s durational requirements, evidence of
                                                                                         6
                                          Case 5:25-cv-00387-BLF           Document 58         Filed 08/26/26     Page 7 of 9




                                       unreported defects may tend to prove whether the Subject Vehicle was fit for its “ordinary
                                   1

                                   2   purposes.” For these reasons, MIL No. 2 to exclude evidence of unreported complaints is

                                   3   DENIED as to Ms. Zapien’s claim under § 1791.1, but without prejudice to reasserting the
                                   4   objection at trial.
                                   5
                                               C. MIL No. 3 to Exclude Evidence, Testimony, or Argument Relating to
                                   6              Nonconformities in the Subject Vehicle that Arose Outside the Warranty Period

                                   7           In its MIL No. 3, FCA moves to exclude evidence of “complaints, concerns, repairs, or
                                   8
                                       maintenance visits . . . that arose outside the manufacturer’s warranty period.” ECF No. 32 at 2.
                                   9
                                       FCA argues that the Song-Beverly Act excludes nonconformities that arose “outside the
                                  10
                                       manufacturer’s warranty period,” making such evidence irrelevant. Id. at 2–3. FCA further
                                  11

                                  12   maintains that allowing Ms. Zapien to admit evidence of out-of-warranty defects and maintenance
Northern District of California
 United States District Court




                                  13   visits would confuse the jury by artificially “inflat[ing] the repair history.” Id. at 3. In opposition,
                                  14   Ms. Zapien contends that defects arising outside the warranty period can tend to prove whether
                                  15
                                       prior repair attempts successfully cured the nonconformities and whether “latent defect[s] existed
                                  16
                                       during the implied-warranty period.” ECF No. 52 at 3.
                                  17

                                  18           The Court agrees with Plaintiff on two separate grounds. First, evidence that a defect was

                                  19   cured during the warranty period “but reappear[ed] at a later date is relevant to determining

                                  20   whether a fundamental problem in the vehicle was ever resolved.” Donlen, 217 Cal. App. 4th at
                                  21
                                       149. Even where “a defect first appears after a warranty has expired,” it “does not necessarily
                                  22
                                       mean the defect did not exist when the product was purchased.” Id. (emphasis in original).
                                  23
                                       Therefore, “[p]ostwarranty repair evidence may be admitted on a case-by-case basis where it is
                                  24

                                  25   relevant to showing the vehicle was not repaired to conform to the warranty during the warranty’s

                                  26   existence.” Id.
                                  27

                                  28
                                                                                          7
                                          Case 5:25-cv-00387-BLF           Document 58         Filed 08/26/26   Page 8 of 9




                                               Second, at this stage, the Court cannot determine which warranty periods apply to which
                                   1

                                   2   nonconformities. The warranty contract included several express warranties. ECF No. 1.1 at ¶ 8,

                                   3   Ex. A at 7–11. These warranties ran for varying lengths of time and covered different parts of the

                                   4   Subject Vehicle. Id. Without additional evidence, the Court is unable to determine which
                                   5
                                       warranty period applies to which alleged defect. Accordingly, FCA’s MIL No. 3 to deny evidence
                                   6
                                       of repairs or defects occurring outside the warranty period is DENIED without prejudice to
                                   7
                                       reasserting it in response to specific evidence at trial.
                                   8
                                               D. MIL No. 4 to Exclude Evidence, Testimony, or Argument on Recall Service Visits
                                   9

                                  10           FCA’s MIL No. 4 seeks to exclude testimony or argument that “characterize[s] recall-only

                                  11   service visits as attempts to repair” nonconformities where the Subject Vehicle “was presented
                                  12   solely for performance of a recall.” ECF No. 33 at 2. FCA asserts that recall work may be
Northern District of California
 United States District Court




                                  13
                                       performed regardless of whether a vehicle has the defect that triggered the recall, making the
                                  14
                                       probative value of recall-only service visits negligible. Id. at 3–4. In particular, FCA moves to
                                  15
                                       “exclude evidence of the following recalls: Y67 performed on January 30, 2023 (Repair Order
                                  16

                                  17   #115133), 13A performed on August 7, 2023, and ZA3, Y43, and S43 performed on June 13,

                                  18   2025 (Repair Order #297259).” Id. at 3.

                                  19           In opposition, Ms. Zapien alleges that FCA’s MIL No. 4 mischaracterized the January 30,
                                  20   2023, and August 7, 2023, service visits because those visits were not limited to recall work. ECF
                                  21
                                       No. 53 at 2. Ms. Zapien also argues that evidence of recall work is relevant because the recall
                                  22
                                       campaigns may be related to the reported defects in the Subject Vehicle. Id. at 3.
                                  23
                                               The Court agrees that evidence of recall work may be relevant to Ms. Zapien’s claims. As
                                  24

                                  25   Ms. Zapien notes, whether the specified service visits were limited to recall work is a fact-specific

                                  26   inquiry for the jury to decide. Evidence of recall visits may also tend to prove whether the defects

                                  27   that triggered the recall were present in the Subject Vehicle. For example, as discussed during the
                                  28
                                       hearing, one of the recall campaigns concerned “an engine-compartment fire risk associated with
                                                                                       8
                                         Case 5:25-cv-00387-BLF           Document 58         Filed 08/26/26     Page 9 of 9




                                       the grid-heater relay.” Id. at 3. Meanwhile, one of the complaints that Ms. Zapien allegedly
                                   1

                                   2   presented to FCA’s representative was a concern about a “burning odor.” Id. The fire-related

                                   3   recall campaign may provide circumstantial evidence that the burning odor was caused by a

                                   4   defective grid-heater relay. For these reasons, FCA’s MIL No. 4 to exclude evidence of recall-
                                   5
                                       only visits is DENIED without prejudice to reasserting this objection at trial.
                                   6
                                       IV.    ORDER
                                   7
                                              For the foregoing reasons, IT IS HEREBY ORDERED that:
                                   8
                                              (1) FCA’s MIL No. 1 to exclude evidence of complaints that were repaired after one
                                   9

                                  10              service visit is DENIED without prejudice to reasserting the objection at trial.

                                  11          (2) FCA’s MIL No. 2 to exclude evidence of complaints that Ms. Zapien never reported to
                                  12              FCA’s authorized representatives is GRANTED as to Ms. Zapien’s claim under Cal.
Northern District of California
 United States District Court




                                  13
                                                  Civ. Code § 1793.2(d)(2) and DENIED without prejudice to reasserting the objection
                                  14
                                                  at trial as to Ms. Zapien’s claim under Cal. Civ. Code § 1791.1.
                                  15
                                              (3) FCA’s MIL No. 3 to exclude evidence of repairs and defects occurring outside the
                                  16

                                  17              warranty period is DENIED without prejudice to reasserting the objection at trial.

                                  18          (4) FCA’s MIL No. 4 to exclude evidence characterizing recall-only service visits as repair

                                  19              attempts is DENIED without prejudice to reasserting the objection at trial.
                                  20          (5) This order terminates ECF Nos. 30, 31, 32, 33.
                                  21
                                              IT IS SO ORDERED.
                                  22

                                  23

                                  24   Dated: August 26, 2026

                                  26                                                    United States District Judge
